name: Fluency heuristic
statement: When two familiar options are compared, the one retrieved faster is inferred to be the larger, and speed of retrieval stands in for knowledge about either.
meaning: Two claims sit inside the name and they have different amounts of evidence behind them. The narrow one is a decision rule for paired comparisons: if both objects are recognised and one comes to mind more quickly, choose that one and consult nothing else. Schooler and Hertwig defined it that way, as the successor to the recognition heuristic for the cases the recognition heuristic cannot touch, and they operationalised fluency as recognition latency. The wide one is that ease of processing, from any source, feeds any judgment. Repetition, high contrast, rhyme and simple pronunciation all make a stimulus easier to take in, and the ease is then misread as evidence that the stimulus is true, liked, safe or big. Alter and Oppenheimer's review calls the wide version a ubiquitous metacognitive cue and groups conceptual, perceptual and linguistic fluency together on the grounds that they produce similar judgments. The narrow rule can be measured against a model. The wide claim cannot, and its parts have fared differently.

origin.who: Lael J. Schooler and Ralph Hertwig
origin.note: Their paper is "How Forgetting Aids Heuristic Inference", and it names and formalises the heuristic inside the ACT-R architecture rather than testing it on people. Schooler and Hertwig trace the underlying idea to Jacoby and colleagues, citing Jacoby and Dallas, Jacoby and Brooks, and Kelley and Jacoby. They cite the false fame effect to Jacoby, Kelley, Brown and Jasechko, and the perceived truth of repeated assertions to Begg, Anas and Farinacci, as cases where fluency already acts as a cue.

evidence: The 2005 paper is a simulation. Applied to all pairs of the 83 largest German cities, with ACT-R's default decay rate of -.50, the fluency heuristic answered 62.1% correctly against the recognition heuristic's 61.3%. Fluency validity, the chance of a correct answer when both cities are recognised, was .61, well below the recognition validity of .82. Performance peaked at an intermediate decay rate of -.25, and the fluency rule's own validity peaked at -.42, so forgetting helped by spreading retrieval times far enough apart to be told apart. The human evidence arrived in 2008. Hertwig, Herzog, Schooler and Reimer ran four studies. In the second, 120 students judged which of two names they had recognised faster; for gaps above 100 ms they scored a median .76, and below 100 ms accuracy sat at .53, with a 95% confidence interval from .49 to .58. In the third, 80 students at the Free University of Berlin made 156 paired comparisons. Choices matched the heuristic in .74 of applicable cases for US cities, .63 for German companies and .68 for music artists, against individual baselines that were 16, 11 and 15 percentage points lower, d = 1.03, 0.83 and 1.38. The heuristic was applicable to between 23% and 33% of inferences. In the fourth, 50 students at Basel counted syllables in a set of city names, which raised the chance of picking those cities as larger to .55, SD = .13, 95% CI [.52, .59], t(49) = 2.94, p = .005, d = .37.

examples.tag: Two rivers on a quiz sheet
examples.text: Asked which of two rivers is longer, a quizzer picks the one whose name arrived first. Both names were recognised and neither length is known, so the speed of retrieval has stood in for the fact the question asked for.

A new employee is asked which of two teams has more staff and names the one that came to mind quickest. Both were covered at the induction, so the answer rests on which surfaced sooner rather than on any headcount.

examples.tag: The charity that sprang to mind first
examples.text: Deciding which of two charities is the larger, a donor goes with the one whose name arrived faster. Both are recognised, and nothing known about either organisation's size entered the judgement.

replication.headline: The choice pattern reproduces in other laboratories at about two thirds of applicable pairs. Model-based estimates put decisions made on fluency alone at about one in five.
replication.detail: Pohl, Erdfelder, Michalkiewicz, Castela and Hilbig reanalysed 21 data sets to ask whether the standard procedures inflate or deflate estimates of use. Neither the order of the recognition and inference tasks nor repeated presentation of the objects mattered: 12 of 17 data sets showed no difference in estimated use across task orders, with average probabilities of .19 and .22, and 19 of 21 showed none across first and last presentations, in studies presenting objects as often as 24 times. They conclude that use of the heuristic on about 20% of pairs of recognised objects is plausible, and that the estimate is stable across the procedural variations they tested. The separation that matters is between adherence and use. Adherence, the proportion of applicable pairs in which the faster-recognised object was chosen, is reliably above chance and runs at about two thirds. Pohl and colleagues give .63 and .68 for two of their own data sets, against the .63, .68 and .74 of Hertwig and colleagues' third study. Use, the probability that the choice was made on fluency and nothing else, is estimated by a multinomial processing tree called the r-s model. Hilbig, Erdfelder and Pohl's abstract calls the fluency heuristic an unlikely candidate for describing comparative judgments concerning recognised objects. The s estimates behind that are .23 in Hilbig and colleagues' 2011 study, .16 in Schwikert and Curran's first experiment and .21 in their second. All are small and all are above zero. The 2011 figure is quoted here as Pohl and colleagues report it; Schwikert and Curran's two were read in their own paper, where they sit against adherence rates of .588 and .62 in the same samples. That paper recruited 59 people for the first experiment and analysed 48, and ran 34 in the second. The model-based tests agree with each other. So the behaviour is there and the single-cue account of it is not.

study.cite: Pohl, R. F., Erdfelder, E., Michalkiewicz, M., Castela, M., & Hilbig, B. E. (2016). The limited use of the fluency heuristic: Converging evidence across different procedures. Memory & Cognition, 44(7), 1114-1126.

limits: Fluency is a weak cue where it applies. Across the 18 remaining data sets in Pohl and colleagues' reanalysis the mean fluency validity was .57, with a range from .44 to .67. Knowledge validity for the same pairs averaged .65, ranging from .57 to .74, and was greater than fluency validity in 16 of the 21 sets. Pohl and colleagues also report a mean fluency validity of .62 across 25 data sets in Herzog and Hertwig's overview, and .55 in Volz and colleagues' study. Those two figures were not checked against their own papers. Pohl and colleagues write that every empirical study of the heuristic has used recognition speed as the proxy for retrieval fluency, and that objective speed and subjective fluency can come apart. They quote Reber and colleagues' 2004 line that there seemingly is no single objective fluency. The samples are German, Swiss and American students. The objects are cities, companies, athletes, music artists and wealthy people. No direct repeat of the 2008 syllable-counting experiment was found on 21 September 2026. That search covered Crossref by title and by DOI, the Semantic Scholar citation lists of the 2008 paper and of Pohl and colleagues, and the open web under both the 'fluency heuristic' and 'retrieval fluency' names. OpenAlex was tried on the same day and refused the query on rate limits. What the search did turn up is later work on neighbouring models rather than on the manipulation: Castela and Erdfelder's memory state heuristic, which reads recognition latency as memory strength rather than fluency, and Xu and colleagues' familiarity difference cue, which has its own entry at 256. The Castela and Erdfelder paper was opened far enough to confirm that it tests a rival model and not the syllable manipulation, and no figure is taken from it here.
misreadings: The name is used for two things and only one of them has been measured this way. Within this atlas, four neighbouring entries are all sometimes called fluency effects, and their records differ. Repetition raising rated truth has survived: Ye and colleagues pooled 366 effect sizes from 182 studies in 99 articles, covering 31,184 participants, and after a PEESE correction for small-study effects put the illusory truth effect at g = 0.37, 95% CI [0.30, 0.44]. That is entry 27. Fluency raising liking has support beyond repetition, since Reber, Winkielman and Schwarz raised liking across three experiments by priming, by figure-ground contrast and by presentation duration, which is the two-step account behind the mere-exposure effect. The mere-exposure record itself is mixed, as entry 21 sets out. Rhyme raising rated accuracy has no independent repeat, as entry 123 records. Disfluency improving reasoning has failed: in Many Labs 2 the hard-to-read font produced d = -0.03, 95% CI [-0.08, 0.01], across the aggregate replication sample of 6,935 participants, and entry 20 gives the confirmatory subsample. Inferring rank from which of two recognised objects feels more familiar, rather than from which arrives faster, is entry 256. The record outside this atlas is uneven in the same way. Song and Schwarz found ostensible food additives with hard-to-pronounce names rated more harmful, with 20 students in one study and 15 in another. Bahnik and Vranka built new names by the same recipe, recruiting 616 online workers for one preregistered study and analysing 572, and recruiting 200 people for a laboratory study and analysing 186. The effect held for Song and Schwarz's original items, b = -0.48, 95% CI [-0.79, -0.17], and vanished for the new ones, b = -0.11, 95% CI [-0.39, 0.16]. In their amusement-park study, which recruited 1,042 and analysed 950, name length predicted perceived risk, b = 0.71, 95% CI [0.44, 0.98], while pronounceability did not. A second error is to read adherence as use. Two thirds of choices agreeing with a heuristic does not mean two thirds of choices were made by it, because the faster-recognised object is usually also the better-known one. A third is to treat the 2005 result as data. It is an ACT-R simulation of German cities, and its 62.1% is a model's score, not a person's.
